posts.author: Khaldriel
posts.body:
This seems... odd.
I get that they were mixing RTPs to show that the new Maker might allow for multiple resource types. But the actual presentation is quite rough around the edges.
Here are a few things that stood out to me:
First,
it looks like shadows cannot be cast towards the camera in this version. Even with several light sources present, everything is casting shadows forward. This makes me think that they might not allow players to rotate the camera or adjust its angle.
Second,
the shadow quality is quite low and as can be seen on the walls to the right, some shadows get cut off in a strange way.
Third,
the look is inconsistent. There are circular shadows under the trees, while other objects cast 'proper' shadows (though the lamp shadows are actually reversed if you pay attention to their shape). It creates a weird contrast between objects that have "dynamic" shadows and those that don't.
Fourth,
the angle of some objects is plainly wrong. The base of the lamp posts looks diagonal instead of sitting properly on the surface (unlike the boxes, which look proportionally correct given the camera angle).
So, I guess for a first showing, they could have done much more, taking into account that nobody was rushing them to release this.
Also I wouldn't worry about them not releasing a new RTP, this was made this way to show that people can use old resources in my opinion.
It could be good, but as we all know with the RPG Maker series, it often feels like one step forward and two steps back. I hope this time they finally get it right.

Most likely this won't work for them - not without a lot of problems that I hope they are intelligent enough to see before trying.
Office programs (Microsoft) or image programs (Adobe) can get away with a subscription model because they have a quick turnaround in productivity. You need them every month and produce something of value in a few hours/days max.
Most games need years to be created, and I strongly doubt that anyone is willing to pay a subscription for years before they can release their game - not unless it is a very minor subscription, and that would simply cause more loss to them due to transaction fees than they would get.
They might get around that by offering only yearly subscription fees instead of monthly, but that is still a high risk given the usual clientele for the makers.
The only real alternative in payment models would have been to ask for royalties on completed and sold games like several other companies do with their engines. But that would mean that they basically have to give away the engine and wait a year or two to get the first royalties on the first games completed.
They might have been able to do that if they tried it with Unite, but after two flops I doubt they have the reserves needed for such a delay, they need a good product to sell soon.
